episodes.title: Episode 07: Is the GA undertrained?
notes: +1000 generations from the released genomes: Witch 49.5%, Mine 50.5% vs their v2 selves (held-out, 8000 games); Gardens flat
Specialists trained from scratch in round 2 were undertrained: Workshop 52.7%, Vassal 54.9% vs v2 (+2-3 pts vs bots)
Swapping them into portfolio-v2: 50.1% +-0.9 over 300 fresh kingdoms; the GA base never uses them
Training against the RL network (rl_r2_200, weight 2): Witch 41.6% vs net, v2 42.4% - no gain
Conclusion: the main specialists are at the genome's ceiling; training stopped
transcript: You asked a fair question. The genetic algorithm behind the portfolio is the baseline every newer model is measured against. The reinforcement learning network beats it about seventy percent of the time. So maybe the baseline is weak only because it never trained long enough. Today I tested that, and the answer is mostly no.

Here is what I looked at first. Each specialist in portfolio version two trained for five hundred generations. Most of them had flat curves at the end. But a few were still climbing. Mine, Vassal, Workshop and Witch had all gained between three and five points in their last hundred generations. That looked like a model that stopped too early.

So I took the released specialists and kept training them, one thousand more generations each, with the same settings. Every twenty five generations the run saved its best genome. Then I measured each saved genome on games no run had ever seen. Four thousand games against the bots, and eight thousand head to head against the version two specialist it started from.

Witch did not move. After a thousand generations it won forty nine and a half percent against its old self. Mine won fifty and a half. Gardens stayed flat on the training scores the whole time. These specialists had already trained in an earlier round, so in total they have a thousand generations behind them, and they have stopped.

Two specialists did get better. Workshop won fifty two point seven percent against its old version, and Vassal fifty four point nine. Both also scored two to three points more against the bots. That is well outside the noise. What they have in common is that they were trained from scratch in round two, with only five hundred generations. So you were right about those two. They were undertrained.

But does that make the baseline stronger? I swapped the better Workshop and Vassal into the portfolio and played it against the original on three hundred fresh kingdoms. Fifty point one percent. No difference. The portfolio rarely picks those two, and the baseline the other models are measured against never uses them at all. That baseline mostly plays Witch, Militia, Gardens, Market and Bandit, and those are the ones that no longer improve.

Then I tried your other idea, training against the best model instead of only the bots. I plugged the reinforcement learning network into the genetic algorithm as an opponent, weighted twice as much as a bot. The Witch specialist trained against it for four hundred generations. It never found anything better. Against the network it scored forty one and a half percent, and the starting genome forty two. The net is a stronger teacher, but the student can't learn what it teaches.

So the lesson repeats what episode six suspected, now with a direct test. A buy list in three phases has a ceiling, and the main specialists have reached it. More generations and a stronger opponent both leave them where they are. The only real gains were in specialists that started late, and they barely matter to the portfolio.

I stopped all the training, as you asked, when it stopped paying off. The useful leftovers are a measurement script for specialists, a fix that lets the trainer use evolved opponents on the new Python version, and the two better specialists, which are not released. If the baseline is going to get stronger, it has to be a different kind of player, like the search from last episode, not more of the same evolution.

episodes.title: Episode 06: When training stops helping, search
notes: Round 3 (league training) tied portfolio-v2 (50.4%) and was stopped; endgame rule 49.8%, money gate 50.0%, bigger pool 50.1%: the GA genome is saturated
Longer specialist trial (300 games per opponent): pick vs bots 80.4% -> 81.0%, now on
Rollout search on top of the specialists (C engine continues a copied game): 64.0% vs the same specialist, 2000 games
Search needs the opponent's cards: the autopilot now tracks them from the opponent's 'Added:' banner (57.7% even with 25% missed)
portfolio-v2s published as opt-in; not yet played on Steam
transcript: This morning portfolio version two was the new default. It won fifty seven percent of games against version one. You asked me to keep improving the model, so this episode is about what I tried, what failed, and the one thing that worked.

First, a third round of training. Every specialist trained against the best specialists of round two, like a league. It made no difference. Halfway through, the new portfolio tied version two, fifty percent to fifty. So I stopped it.

Then four smaller ideas. An endgame rule that looks at the score: buy the last Province only if it wins, and never if it loses. It changed nothing, forty nine point eight percent. A rule to wait for enough money before buying Provinces. The evolved buy lists already do that, so the rule almost never fired. A bigger pool, with version one and version two specialists together. Again fifty percent. A longer trial before each game, to pick the right specialist. That one helped a little, half a point, and it is now on.
The lesson is that the specialists have reached what their strategy can express. A fixed list of what to buy, in three phases, can only get so good. More training of the same kind won't change that.

So I built a different kind of player on top of them, called rollout search. At every buy, it takes the specialist's choice, its next few choices, and buying nothing. For each one, it plays the rest of the game out three hundred times in the fast engine, with the cards it can't see shuffled at random. Then it picks the option that wins most often. But it only overrules the specialist when the difference is clear.
To make that possible, the engine learned to copy a game in the middle of a turn and continue it. A test checks that a copied game finishes exactly like the original.

The first try was worse, about forty four percent, because with only thirty playouts the differences are mostly luck. With three hundred playouts and a small margin, the search wins sixty four percent of games against the same specialist without search. That is over two thousand games, and it's the biggest gain in the whole project.

There is one condition. The search needs to know what is in the opponent's deck. When it had to imagine the opponent as a copy of its own deck, the gain disappeared. On Steam, though, the opponent's bar at the top of the screen says Added, and the card, every time they gain one. So the autopilot now reads that banner and keeps count of the opponent's cards. In simulation, even if it misses a quarter of them, the search still wins about fifty eight percent.

The new model is called portfolio version two s, with s for search. It is published, but it isn't the default yet. It has not played a real Steam game, and that game takes over the mouse, so it waits until you say go.
So what's next is simple. Watch a few real games with the search model. Check that the opponent count matches the card counter on screen. If it holds up, it becomes the default.

episodes.title: Episode 05: Every card on Steam, and a stronger model overnight
notes: All 26 base-set cards are playable on Steam: protocol 2 asks the model for every card's own choice, and the autopilot learned each prompt in 4 games (Sentry needs drag and drop)
Bugs fixed on the way: Militia '(0 of 2)' counter, an unseen empty Estate pile clicked 58 times, the agent keeping a Province over Gold
First real game with all cards: portfolio-v1 picked its Gardens + Workshop specialist and won 34-33 vs Easy
Overnight round 2 (26 specialists vs bots + strong round-1 specialists) -> portfolio-v2: 57.1% head to head vs v1, 81.0% vs bots
Generalist with 4x the budget plateaued: the genome is its limit
transcript: Last time, the new model was a portfolio. It is a set of specialists, one built around Witch, one around Militia, one around Gardens, and so on. When a game starts, it tries every specialist on the cards that were dealt, and the best one plays. But nine cards were still blocked. The autopilot could not answer the questions Steam asks when you play them, so no model was allowed to buy them. You asked me to fix that, and then to keep improving the model through the night.

The fix had two halves. The first half was the model side. Every card that asks you something now has its own question in the protocol. Remodel asks what to trash and what to gain. Cellar asks what to discard. Sentry asks what to do with the top two cards of your deck. Each answer comes from the same code the model trained with. A test plays three hundred games in the engine, and at every one of these choices it checks that the answer the autopilot would get is exactly what the model did in training. They matched every time.

The second half was the screen. I had to learn how Steam actually asks. So the autopilot played four games against the easiest computer player, with a test model that buys all the new cards. Every time it met a screen it did not know, it saved a picture and stopped. Then I taught it that screen and let it continue. Gaining a card is a click on a glowing pile. Cellar is a choice of cards and then OK, or a button called Decline. Harbinger and Vassal show a small window to pick from. Library has a button called Set Aside. Sentry was the surprise. You have to drag the cards into zones called trash, discard and deck. So the autopilot learned to drag.

Those games found several old bugs too. A Militia attack shows a counter, zero of two, and the autopilot read that zero as the number of cards to discard. When an empty pile was not noticed, Workshop clicked it fifty eight times in a row. And the model itself, when attacked by Militia, kept a Province in hand and threw away a Gold. All of these are fixed.

Then came a real game, with all cards allowed, against the easy computer player. The portfolio looked at the kingdom and picked its Gardens and Workshop specialist, which could never be used before. It won, thirty four to thirty three.

Overnight came the second round of training. In the first round, every specialist learned against three simple scripted opponents. This time each one also had to beat three strong specialists from the first round. Twenty six specialists trained this way, about fifteen minutes each. Together they form portfolio version two, now the default.

The best test is a match. Both portfolios look at the same random kingdom, each picks its own specialist, and they play each other. Over two hundred kingdoms, version two wins fifty seven percent of the games. Against the simple opponents both are close to the limit, eighty one percent against eighty.

One experiment failed. I gave the generalist, the specialist for any kingdom, four times as much training. It did not improve at all after the first quarter. So its limit is the shape of its strategy, not training time.

Two rare screens were never seen yet. One is revealing a Moat when attacked, and the other is choosing which treasure a Bandit takes. Next is a third round, where the new specialists train against each other, and then real games against the hard computer player.

episodes.title: Episode 04: One engine for every model, and how the pieces fit
notes: Steam campaign: 5 won, 6 lost of 11 finished games (Very Easy/Easy 4 of 5, Medium 1 of 3, Hard 0 of 3), model k1-steam
The old simulator differed from Steam: 12 Provinces instead of 8, 15 of 26 cards, a turn-40 cap, ties as half a win
New shared engine with Steam's rules and all 26 cards, Python + C; 1,500 random games compared decision by decision, zero differences
Setup: engine/ (the game) -> trainers/ga-v1/ (evolves and releases models) -> autopilot/ (reads the kingdom, the selector picks a model, clicks)
All models re-benchmarked on Steam rules; nine new cards (Cellar, Remodel...) are not bought until the autopilot can answer their prompts
transcript: Since the last episode, the autopilot played a full campaign on Steam. Eleven games were finished. It won five and lost six. Against the two easiest computer players it won four of five, and the one loss was caused by a bug in the autopilot, which is now fixed. Against the medium player it won one of three. Against the hard player it lost all three, by two, eight and eighteen points.

The reason was clear from the games. The hard player ends the game fast, in about twenty turns. Our model builds a slow money deck, and it ignores most kingdom cards. In a typical game, about six of the ten kingdom cards were cards it had never learned.

That led to a bigger finding. The simulator the strategies were evolved in did not play quite the same game as Steam. It used twelve Provinces in a two player game, and Steam uses eight. It knew fifteen of the twenty six kingdom cards. Every simulated game stopped at turn forty. And a tie counted as half a win, while Steam gives the win to the player who took fewer turns. So the models were trained for a slightly different game.

Today that was fixed at the root. The game itself is now its own project, called the engine. It plays Dominion the way Steam does, with all twenty six cards. It exists twice, once in Python, which is easy to read, and once in C, which is about sixty times faster for training. Both versions shuffle the same way and ask the same questions in the same order. A test plays fifteen hundred random games in both and compares every single decision. There were no differences.
Here is how the whole setup fits together. Think of three pieces in a row.

The first piece is the engine. It is the rules and nothing else. Every choice in a game, like which action to play, what to buy, or what to discard to a Militia, is asked as one question with a list of answers. Anything that can answer those questions can play. That could be a simple bot, an evolved strategy, you in the game window, or later a neural network.

The second piece is a trainer. Right now there is one, the genetic algorithm. It plays millions of games on the engine and evolves a strategy. When a strategy is good, it is released as a model. A model is just a folder. It holds the evolved strategy, the kingdom it was trained on, its key cards, and a benchmark score. The key cards are the kingdom cards it is built around. The benchmark is how often it beats three fixed opponents on two hundred random kingdoms. All the models were benchmarked again today on the new engine. The strongest one is still the model built around Witch and Market, at about eighty percent.

The third piece is the autopilot. It reads the Steam screen and clicks. When a game starts, it reads the ten kingdom cards from the game's save file. Then a selector picks the model for that kingdom. First choice is a model trained on exactly those cards. Next is a model whose key cards were all dealt, with the best benchmark. A model only ever buys cards it was trained with, so the right model matters.

On disk, this is three folders. The engine folder holds the game. The trainers folder holds one folder per kind of model, and the genetic algorithm lives in one called ga v one. A future neural network would get its own folder right next to it. The autopilot folder holds the screen reading, the control panel, and this website. Each trainer pins the exact version of the engine it trained on.
One honest limit. For nine of the new cards, like Cellar and Remodel, the autopilot can't yet answer the questions Steam asks when you play them. So for now, no model is allowed to buy those nine.
What's next is clear. Train new models on the new engine, with the real rules and all the cards. Then send them back into the campaign, and see if they can finally beat the hard player.

episodes.title: Episode 03: What three games taught, and how to run it
notes: Bug: the tilted leftmost card was read upside down (SMITHY -> AHLIWS); fixed by turning off the OCR orientation check for the hand
First fix was wrong: it passed a faked test, failed on the real frame
Bug: empty Duchy/Estate piles stalled game 2 for 27 turns; fixed by checking coins/buys after each buy click
Results vs Very Easy AI: 58-8, 76-7, 55-35
The strategy's late game (Silver over Gold, buys Copper) is weak in long games: trained with a 40-turn cap
transcript: In the first episode, the autopilot won its first game fifty eight to eight. That game was clean. The next two games were recorded, frame by frame, to make the films. And the recordings found problems that a clean game had hidden.

The first problem was a card that was read upside down. The card at the far left of your hand is drawn tilted. Once in a while, the text reader decided it was upside down, and turned it over before reading. Smithy came out as a h l i w s. With no action card found, the autopilot ended its action phase and bought nothing with two coins. That happened twice in the second game.

My first fix was wrong, and I want to be honest about that. I read the unmatched word again, turned upside down. It passed my test, but my test had flipped the picture by hand. On the real frame, the fix made it worse. In the third game, Smithy was skipped again on turn six. The real fix was simpler. Hand cards are never upside down, so the reader's turning check is now off for the hand. After that, every Smithy was read and played.

The second problem was stranger. In the second game, the provinces stayed at two for twenty seven turns. The autopilot kept buying a Duchy or an Estate every turn. But those piles were empty. Clicking an empty pile does nothing, so every turn ended without a purchase. The strategy had never seen this in training, because its simulator always knows when a pile runs out. The fix is a small check. After every buy click, the autopilot compares the coins and buys with what they were before. If nothing changed, the pile is empty, and it asks the strategy again without that card. Restarted with that fix, it found both empty piles in two turns, went back to buying treasure, and won seventy six to seven.

In the third game the same check worked from the start. The Estate pile ran out on turn twenty five, and the autopilot noticed after one click. That game ended on three empty piles, and it won fifty five to thirty five.

The long games also showed a weak spot in the strategy itself. In its late phase it prefers Silver to Gold, and with one or two coins it still buys Copper. So a long late game fills the deck with weak cards, and eight coins become rare. In training this hardly mattered, because every simulated game stops at turn forty. That is a lesson for the next round of evolution, not a bug in the autopilot.
So, three games against the very easy computer player, and three wins.

If you want to run it yourself, it takes about five minutes. Clone the repository with its submodule. Make a Python virtual environment, and install the five packages from the requirements file. Start Dominion from Steam, and begin a game against the computer. Leave the window at its normal size and in plain view. Then run the pilot script, and keep your hand off the mouse. The film called How to run it shows every step, and the site lists every option.

Two habits help. Start with the dry option once. It reads and decides without clicking, so you can check the log against what you see. And if something goes wrong, look in the unknown folder. Anything the autopilot didn't understand is saved there as a picture.

That's where things stand. The autopilot plays whole games on its own. Its main limit now is the strategy, which only knows fifteen cards and has a weak late game. Both of those are jobs for the genetic algorithm, not for the eyes and hands.

episodes.title: Episode 02: How it sees, decides and clicks
notes: One prompt per loop pass: screenshot until still, read the prompt line, run its handler
Hand names are fuzzy-matched (>= 80% similar) to this game's cards; counters give actions, coins, buys
Buys come from dominion-v1's own play_buy_phase on a stand-in state (buy targets + terminal density included)
Clicks: glide, rest 0.35 s, press and hold 0.15 s, via XTEST
Memory per game in autopilot/run_<seed>.json; rematch with --games N
transcript: This episode goes through the autopilot one part at a time, in the order it works during a turn. If you want to see it, the film called How it works shows the same steps on recorded footage.
Everything runs in one loop. Each pass handles exactly one thing the game asks for. And each pass has three parts. The eyes, the brain, and the hands.

The eyes start with a screenshot of the game window. Before it reads anything, the autopilot takes a second screenshot a third of a second later. It compares the two. If they differ, the game is still moving, so it waits and tries again. Only a still screen gets read.

Then it reads the prompt line. That is the sentence just under the supply. It says things like play action cards, play treasure cards, or buy a card. The prompt decides which handler runs next. A prompt it doesn't recognise is saved as a picture, and the autopilot waits for you.

If the prompt asks for actions, it reads the hand. Every card has its name on a banner at the top, and the text reader returns each name with its position. Those positions are where it will click later. The names are matched against the cards in this game. A small reading mistake, like State instead of Estate, still matches, as long as the two are eighty percent alike or more.

Next it reads the counters. They are three small numbers left of the hand, for actions, coins and buys. In the action phase it waits until the actions counter shows at least one, because a zero means the turn is still starting.

Now the brain. The evolved strategy splits the game into three phases. In this model the early phase is just the first two turns. The middle lasts until only two provinces are left, or until turn sixteen. After that comes the late phase. Each phase has its own buy list. Early, it wants Smithy above everything. In the middle, Province, then Gold, then Silver. Late, Province, then Duchy.

For actions it keeps two lists. Cards that give back an action, like Merchant or Market, are played first. Then the terminal cards, like Smithy. It skips a Moneylender when there is no Copper in hand to trash.

Buying is the part I am most careful about. The autopilot doesn't re-write the buy rules. It builds a stand-in game state. That state holds the coins and buys it just read, the cards it owns, and a supply without the cards the strategy never learned. Then it calls the buy function from the original training engine, and uses whatever that function buys. This brings along two rules that are easy to forget. One caps how many copies of a card to own. The other refuses a terminal action card when the deck has no spare actions to play it.

The hands come last. Clicks are sent through an X eleven extension called X test. The game only accepts a click after a short hover. So the pointer glides in, rests for about a third of a second, and then presses and holds. Hand cards are clicked a little below their name, on the card itself, because a hovered card lifts up.

Between turns, the autopilot keeps a small memory file named after the game's seed. It holds the turn number, the provinces left, the cards it owns, and any piles it found empty. If you stop it in the middle of a game and start it again, it reads that file and carries on.

At the end, the score screen appears. The autopilot reads the points, saves a picture of the screen, and stops. Or, if you asked for more games, it presses rematch and starts again with the new kingdom.
That is the whole machine. In the next episode, I'll tell you what the recorded games revealed, and how you can run it yourself.

episodes.title: Episode 01: From a simulator to the Steam game
notes: The evolved strategy (dominion-v1) beats Big Money 73% and its hall of fame 54% in its own engine
Steam Dominion runs under Proton as an XWayland window: screenshots (~50 ms) and XTEST clicks work without a permission prompt
The kingdom comes from the game's own save file (gamelocal_*.xml)
Clicks only register after a hover; clicks during animations are lost
First full game: won 58-8 against Very Easy AI in 21 turns
transcript: You asked a simple question. Could the Dominion strategy from your genetic algorithm project play the real Dominion game on Steam? This episode is the story of how it got there, and what was in the way.

The strategy comes from a project that evolved Dominion players inside its own small game engine. It played thousands of games, kept the winners, and mixed and mutated them. What came out is one small file of lists. What to buy early, in the middle, and late. Which action cards to play first. What to trash with a Chapel. In its own engine it beats the simple Big Money strategy about three games in four, and it wins just over half its games against its own hall of fame.

The Steam game is a different world. It is a closed Windows program that runs on Linux through Proton. There is no way for a bot to plug in. No interface, no mods, and no file that lists the cards in your hand. So the only way in was the way a person plays. Look at the screen, decide, and click.

The first worry was the desktop. Your machine runs Wayland, and Wayland is built to stop one program from watching another. But Proton runs the game as an old style X eleven window, inside a layer called X Wayland. Inside that layer, a program can still copy a window's pixels. The first screenshot came back in about a twentieth of a second, with no permission dialog. A test click on the play treasures button worked too. That was the moment the project became possible.

The second piece was knowing the kingdom. Here the game helped. It saves each local game as a small text file, and one line of it lists the ten kingdom cards. So the autopilot never has to recognise the supply. It reads the list, then finds each pile on screen by its name.

Reading the screen is done by a text recognition model called Rapid O C R. It runs on the processor, on a few small regions. The prompt line says what the game wants. The hand shows the cards. And three counters show actions, coins and buys.

Then came the first surprise. The click on the Silver pile did nothing. It turned out the game only accepts a click after the pointer has hovered over the target for a moment. So every click now glides in, rests for about a third of a second, and then presses. After that, buying worked.

The second surprise was timing. At the start of a turn, the game animates, and clicks made during that animation are lost. Smithy sometimes needed three clicks. The fix was to wait for a still screen, and to wait until the actions counter shows at least one.

For the decisions, the autopilot doesn't copy the strategy's rules. It builds a stand-in game state from what it read, and calls the original buy function from the training engine. So the purchases on Steam are exactly the purchases the evolved strategy makes in training.

The first full game was against the very easy computer opponent. The autopilot bought Silver, Smithy, three Golds, and then Province after Province. It won fifty eight to eight, in twenty one turns, without any help.

That is where the first episode ends. The next one goes through every part in detail. The one after that is about what the recorded games revealed, including two bugs that only showed up in real play.
